title: DAPR Data Management and Visualization Pipeline
text:
1 Introduction & Setup
This guidebook is intended to teach the fundamentals of data management and data visualization using R and Python. The guide was created and is maintained by the Data Science and Analytics for Precision Rehabilitation (DAPR) Center, funded by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (P50-HD118603). The original code was written by KRL in R with a rough draft in Python, Google Gemini 3.6 was then used to troubleshoot Python code and bundle all scripts as a Quarto Notebook. Accuracy of all final code was confirmed and didactic comments added by KRL.
The guide walks through basic steps of data management - such importing data, merging files, and calculating variables - to data visualizaton for different purposes - from basic figures for quality assurance, to static figures to publication, to interactive and animated figures.
As our example data set, we will use the openly available Balance Data Set (BDS) from Santos & Duarte (2016). In this study, N=163 younger and older adults stood on a force plate under two different visual conditions (eyes open versus eyes closed) and on two different surfaces (a firm surface and a foam surface) for three trials in each condition (making 12 total trials per participant). Each trial lasted 60 seconds and force plate data were sampled at 100 Hz. This gives us an incredibly rich data set for learning how to manage and visualize data in the rehabilitation sciences (e.g., 163 people x 12 trials x 60 secs x 100 samples per second x 3 different force plate axes).

title: Static Data Visualization
text:
In this section, we walk through the iterative process of building data visualizations. We start with raw observations, layer on aesthetic mappings and summary geometry, aggregate data to account for repeated measures, and conclude with multi-panel publication figures.



We begin by mapping Surface condition to the x-axis and PathLength_Total to the y-axis. This raw point plot reveals the basic distribution of data but suffers from heavy overplotting across conditions.
It is worth noting that plotnine is a package for Python that uses syntax essentially identical to ggplot in R (both plotnine and ggplot are based on Leland Wilkinson’s “Grammar of Graphics” - a layered system to build data visualizations). However, when making this document using Quarto inside of R Studio, I need to call Python functions using reticulate and - for computing reasons I do not fully understand - it is difficult to render plotnine objects through reticulate. Thus, for these examples, I am using matplotlib and seaborn to great plots similar to my ggplot visualizations, but for pragmatic users, it is probably more efficient to learn ggplot/plotnine syntax that is portable across languages.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(GGally)

DATA <- readRDS("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.rds") %>% 
  mutate(Subject = factor(Subject),
         AgeGroup = fct_relevel(AgeGroup, "Young", "Old"))

# Plot 1: Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_point()













Show Code
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

DATA = pd.read_csv("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.csv")
DATA["AgeGroup"] = pd.Categorical(DATA["AgeGroup"], categories=["Young", "Old"], ordered=True)

# Step 1: Basic scatter plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total", color="black", ax=ax)
ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)")
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















To evaluate the effect of visual input, we map Vision to point shape and color while dodging the points along the x-axis to reduce overlap.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Plot 2: Dodged points by Vision condition
ggplot(data = DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Vision, col = Vision),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  theme_bw()













Show Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Step 2: Dodged points by Vision condition
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.stripplot(
    data=DATA, 
    x="Surface", 
    y="PathLength_Total",
    hue="Vision", 
    dodge=True, 
    jitter=0.2, 
    ax=ax
)
ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)")
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















To better summarize central tendency and spread, we overlay boxplots beneath jitter-dodged raw data points and apply a high-contrast, colorblind-friendly palette.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
cbPalette <- c("#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99",
               "#8366BD", "#D1C071", "#F0EAD6", "grey20")

# Plot 3: Boxplots with jitter-dodged points
ggplot(data = DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Vision, col = Vision),
             position = position_jitterdodge(dodge.width = 0.5, jitter.width = 0.2),
             alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Vision), width = 0.5,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
               alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) +
  theme_bw()













Show Code
cbPalette = ["#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99", "#8366BD", "#D1C071", "#F0EAD6", "#333333"]

# Step 3: Boxplots with jitter-dodged points
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
sns.boxplot(
    data=DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Vision",
    palette=cbPalette[:2], boxprops=dict(alpha=0.5), showfliers=False, ax=ax
)
sns.stripplot(
    data=DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Vision",
    dodge=True, jitter=0.2, palette=cbPalette[:2], alpha=0.5, ax=ax
)

# Deduplicate legend entries
handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(handles[:2], labels[:2], title="Vision")
ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)")
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















Because individual trials introduce nested variance, we aggregate data to subject-level means (AVE_DATA). We also refine labels, typography, and legend positioning to polish the figure.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Aggregate trial data to subject-level averages
AVE_DATA <- DATA %>% 
  select(-Trial) %>%
  group_by(Subject, Vision, Surface) %>%
  summarise(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    across(!where(is.numeric), dplyr::first),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot 4: Formatted subject-level summary
ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Vision, col = Vision),
             position = position_jitterdodge(dodge.width = 0.5, jitter.width = 0.2),
             alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Vision), width = 0.5,
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
               alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Postural Sway: Total Path Length by Surface and Vision",
    subtitle = "Mean values aggregated across trials per subject",
    x = "Surface Condition",
    y = "Total Path Length (cm)",
    shape = "Vision Condition", 
    col = "Vision Condition",
    fill = "Vision Condition"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, face = "italic", color = "gray30")
  )













Show Code
AVE_DATA = DATA.groupby(["Subject", "Vision", "Surface", "AgeGroup"], as_index=False).mean(numeric_only=True)

# Step 4: Formatted subject-level summary
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.boxplot(
    data=AVE_DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Vision",
    palette=cbPalette[:2], boxprops=dict(alpha=0.5), showfliers=False, ax=ax
)
sns.stripplot(
    data=AVE_DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Vision",
    dodge=True, jitter=0.2, palette=cbPalette[:2], alpha=0.5, ax=ax
)

handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(handles[:2], labels[:2], title="Vision Condition", loc="upper right")

ax.set_title("Postural Sway: Total Path Length by Surface and Vision\n", fontweight="bold", fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlabel("Surface Condition", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)", fontweight="bold")
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















In this study, Surface and Vision are manipulated within a person (i.e., the are both within-subject variables). A critical peace of information in these studies is how consistent participants are in their individal responses (i.e., does the same person tend to score high/low across conditions). Mathematically, we might calculate an intraclass correlation coefficiant to capture how (dis)similar data from the same person happen to be. Visually, we can add lines to our plot “connecting the dots” for data from the same person. To show individual changes across conditions, we facet by Surface and connect subject points from Open to Closed vision conditions using light gray trajectory lines.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Plot 5: Within-subject lines faceted by Surface
ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = Vision, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Subject), color = "gray75", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_point(aes(group = Subject, shape = Vision, col = Vision), size = 2, alpha = 0.5,
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Vision), width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ Surface) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette[c(1,2)]) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Postural Sway: Within-Subject Visual Effects",
    subtitle = "Lines connect individual subjects from Open to Closed conditions",
    x = "Vision Condition",
    y = "Total Path Length (cm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, face = "italic", color = "gray30"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
  )













Show Code
# Step 5: Within-subject trajectory lines faceted by Surface
vis_palette = {"Open": cbPalette[0], "Closed": cbPalette[1]}
g = sns.FacetGrid(AVE_DATA, col="Surface", height=4.5, aspect=1.1)

for surf_name, ax in g.axes_dict.items():
    sub = AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["Surface"] == surf_name]
    
    # Layer 1: Subject lines
    sns.lineplot(
        data=sub, x="Vision", y="PathLength_Total", units="Subject", 
        estimator=None, color="gray", alpha=0.5, ax=ax
    )
    
    # Layer 2: Overlay scatter points
    sns.scatterplot(
        data=sub, x="Vision", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Vision", 
        style="Vision", palette=vis_palette, s=60, alpha=0.8, legend=False, ax=ax
    )
    
    # Layer 3: Boxplot
    sns.boxplot(
        data=sub, x="Vision", y="PathLength_Total", 
        palette=vis_palette, boxprops=dict(alpha=0.4), showfliers=False, ax=ax
    )
    
    ax.set_title(f"Surface: {surf_name}", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlabel("Vision Condition", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)", fontweight="bold")

g.fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)
g.fig.suptitle("Postural Sway: Within-Subject Visual Effects", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















Next, we evaluate how age group interacts with balance conditions. We plot the combined interaction (Surface:Vision) along the x-axis and facet by AgeGroup.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Create interaction factor for clean aesthetic mapping
AVE_DATA <- AVE_DATA %>% 
  mutate(Condition = interaction(Surface, Vision, sep = ":"))

# Plot 6: Interaction conditions faceted by AgeGroup
ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = Condition, y = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Subject), color = "gray75", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = Condition, col = Condition, group = Subject), 
             size = 2, alpha = 0.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Condition), width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects",
    subtitle = "Lines connect individual subjects across conditions",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total Path Length (cm)",
    shape = "Condition", col = "Condition", fill = "Condition"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, face = "italic", color = "gray30"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold")
  )













Show Code
AVE_DATA["Condition"] = AVE_DATA["Surface"].astype(str) + ":" + AVE_DATA["Vision"].astype(str)
cond_order = ["Firm:Open", "Firm:Closed", "Foam:Open", "Foam:Closed"]
cond_palette = {cond: cbPalette[i] for i, cond in enumerate(cond_order)}

g = sns.FacetGrid(AVE_DATA, col="AgeGroup", height=4.5, aspect=1.2)

for age_group, ax in g.axes_dict.items():
    sub = AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["AgeGroup"] == age_group]
    
    # Layer 1: Subject lines
    sns.lineplot(
        data=sub, x="Condition", y="PathLength_Total", units="Subject", 
        estimator=None, color="gray", alpha=0.5, ax=ax
    )
    # Layer 2: Overlay scatter points
    sns.scatterplot(
        data=sub, x="Condition", y="PathLength_Total", hue="Condition", 
        style="Condition", palette=cond_palette, s=60, alpha=0.8, legend=False, ax=ax
    )
    # Layer 3: Boxplot
    sns.boxplot(
        data=sub, x="Condition", y="PathLength_Total", order=cond_order,
        palette=cond_palette, boxprops=dict(alpha=0.4), showfliers=False, ax=ax
    )
    
    ax.set_title(f"AgeGroup: {age_group}", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Total Path Length (cm)", fontweight="bold")

g.fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8)
g.fig.suptitle("Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)
sns.despine()
plt.show()
















One great feature of programmatic approaches to data visualization is that there are many complex, but relatively common data visualizations that you might want to make. It is often too time consuming to make all of these figures completely from scratch, but fortunately there are many software packages/functions that other people have built that you can readily use. As an example, we will build a multifaceted plot to show the correlations between a set of variables. Visualizing this kind of correlation matrix comes up all the time in data analysis projects - whether you are exploring the data or formally checking mutlicolinearity before building a regression model - so it is a good example to start with here.
To examine all the correlations between our postural metrics across age groups, we build a scatterplot matrix containing bivariate scatter plots comparing each variable to every other variable (lower triangle), density distributions for each variable on its own (diagonal), and correlation coefficients (upper triangle).

R (GGally)Python (seaborn)




Show Code
plot_data <- DATA %>% 
  select(AgeGroup, PathLength_Total, PathLength_ML, PathLength_AP, EllipseArea95) 

# Plot 7: Correlogram matrix
ggpairs(
  data = plot_data,
  columns = 2:5,
  mapping = aes(color = AgeGroup, fill = AgeGroup),
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2)),
  diag = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag", alpha = 0.3)),
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 4))
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )













Show Code
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plot_vars = ["PathLength_Total", "PathLength_ML", "PathLength_AP", "EllipseArea95", "AgeGroup"]
plot_data = DATA[plot_vars]

# Plot 7: Seaborn pairplot matrix
g = sns.pairplot(
    plot_data,
    vars=["PathLength_Total", "PathLength_ML", "PathLength_AP", "EllipseArea95"],
    hue="AgeGroup",
    palette={"Young": cbPalette[0], "Old": cbPalette[1]},
    diag_kind="kde",
    plot_kws={"alpha": 0.4, "s": 20}
)
g.fig.suptitle("Multivariate Correlation Matrix by Age Group", y=1.02, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
















Finally, another common issue that arises in practice is the need to “stitch” multiple panels together into a single figure. People often do this manually using tools like the Gnu Image Manipulation Program or Inkscape (which are open source competitors of tools like Photoshop or Illustrator). It is completely fine to export images into another program to manage/fine tune your layout. However, there are tools in R and Python that allow you to make these kinds of multi-panelled figures. These are great tools to learn because it makes you projects more efficient (e.g., from reading in the data to analysis to final publication-ready figures, you can do it all in one place!).
In the code below, we arrange a few distinct figure types into a multi-panel layout: * Panel A: Age distribution histogram. * Panel B: Directional path length scatter plot (\(\text{PathLength}_{\text{ML}}\) vs \(\text{PathLength}_{\text{AP}}\)) with confidence ellipses. * Panel C: Total path length density distributions by condition faceted across age groups.

R (patchwork)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Panel A: Age Histogram
FigA <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "grey", col = "black", binwidth = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(15, 90), breaks = seq(10, 90, 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))

# Panel B: ML vs AP Path Length Scatter
FigB <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = PathLength_ML, y = PathLength_AP)) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = Condition), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.4, col = "black") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Condition), col = "black", shape = 21, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Path Length M/L (cm)", y = "Path Length A/P (cm)") +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"), legend.position = "none")

# Panel C: Density Distributions by Condition
FigC <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_density(aes(fill = Condition), alpha = 0.4, col = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Total Path Length (cm)", y = "Density") +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

# Combine Panels via Patchwork
((FigA + FigB) / FigC) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A') & 
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 14))













Show Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1, 1])

# Top Row: Panels A and B
ax_a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
ax_b = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])

# Bottom Row: Panel C split by AgeGroup (Young vs Old)
ax_c1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
ax_c2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])

cond_colors = {
    "Firm:Open": cbPalette[0], "Firm:Closed": cbPalette[1],
    "Foam:Open": cbPalette[2], "Foam:Closed": cbPalette[3]
}

# Panel A: Age Histogram
sns.histplot(data=AVE_DATA, x="Age", binwidth=2, color="gray", edgecolor="black", ax=ax_a)
ax_a.set_xlim(15, 90)


(15.0, 90.0)


Show Code
ax_a.set_xlabel("Age (years)", fontweight="bold")
ax_a.set_ylabel("Count", fontweight="bold")
ax_a.set_title("A", loc="left", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)

# Panel B: ML vs AP Path Length Scatter
sns.scatterplot(
    data=AVE_DATA, x="PathLength_ML", y="PathLength_AP",
    hue="Condition", palette=cond_colors, alpha=0.6, edgecolor="black", ax=ax_b
)
ax_b.set_xlabel("Path Length M/L (cm)", fontweight="bold")
ax_b.set_ylabel("Path Length A/P (cm)", fontweight="bold")
ax_b.get_legend().remove()
ax_b.set_title("B", loc="left", fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)

# Panel C1: Density Distribution - Young Adults
sns.kdeplot(
    data=AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["AgeGroup"] == "Young"], x="PathLength_Total", hue="Condition",
    palette=cond_colors, fill=True, common_norm=False, alpha=0.4, ax=ax_c1, legend=False
)
ax_c1.set_xlabel("Total Path Length (cm)", fontweight="bold")
ax_c1.set_ylabel("Density", fontweight="bold")
ax_c1.set_title("Young", fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)
# Add "C" tag to the left density subplot
ax_c1.text(-0.18, 1.05, "C", transform=ax_c1.transAxes, fontweight="bold", fontsize=14)

# Panel C2: Density Distribution - Older Adults
sns.kdeplot(
    data=AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["AgeGroup"] == "Old"], x="PathLength_Total", hue="Condition",
    palette=cond_colors, fill=True, common_norm=False, alpha=0.4, ax=ax_c2
)
ax_c2.set_xlabel("Total Path Length (cm)", fontweight="bold")
ax_c2.set_ylabel("Density", fontweight="bold")
ax_c2.set_title("Old", fontweight="bold", fontsize=11)

# Extract legend handles from ax_c2 and create a clean shared figure legend
handles, labels = ax_c2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax_c2.get_legend().remove()

fig.legend(
    handles, labels, loc="lower center", 
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.01), ncol=4, frameon=False
)

sns.despine()
plt.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.12, hspace=0.35, wspace=0.28)
plt.show()

title: Static Data Visualization
text:
One great feature of programmatic approaches to data visualization is that there are many complex, but relatively common data visualizations that you might want to make. It is often too time consuming to make all of these figures completely from scratch, but fortunately there are many software packages/functions that other people have built that you can readily use. As an example, we will build a multifaceted plot to show the correlations between a set of variables. Visualizing this kind of correlation matrix comes up all the time in data analysis projects - whether you are exploring the data or formally checking mutlicolinearity before building a regression model - so it is a good example to start with here.
To examine all the correlations between our postural metrics across age groups, we build a scatterplot matrix containing bivariate scatter plots comparing each variable to every other variable (lower triangle), density distributions for each variable on its own (diagonal), and correlation coefficients (upper triangle).

R (GGally)Python (seaborn)




Show Code
plot_data <- DATA %>% 
  select(AgeGroup, PathLength_Total, PathLength_ML, PathLength_AP, EllipseArea95) 

# Plot 7: Correlogram matrix
ggpairs(
  data = plot_data,
  columns = 2:5,
  mapping = aes(color = AgeGroup, fill = AgeGroup),
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2)),
  diag = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag", alpha = 0.3)),
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 4))
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# Plot 7: Seaborn pairplot matrix

    plot_data,
    vars=["PathLength_Total", "PathLength_ML", "PathLength_AP", "EllipseArea95"],
    hue="AgeGroup",
    palette={"Young": cbPalette[0], "Old": cbPalette[1]},
    diag_kind="kde",
    plot_kws={"alpha": 0.4, "s": 20}
)
g.fig.suptitle("Multivariate Correlation Matrix by Age Group", y=1.02, fontweight="bold")

title: Static Data Visualization
text:
Finally, another common issue that arises in practice is the need to “stitch” multiple panels together into a single figure. People often do this manually using tools like the Gnu Image Manipulation Program or Inkscape (which are open source competitors of tools like Photoshop or Illustrator). It is completely fine to export images into another program to manage/fine tune your layout. However, there are tools in R and Python that allow you to make these kinds of multi-panelled figures. These are great tools to learn because it makes you projects more efficient (e.g., from reading in the data to analysis to final publication-ready figures, you can do it all in one place!).
In the code below, we arrange a few distinct figure types into a multi-panel layout: * Panel A: Age distribution histogram. * Panel B: Directional path length scatter plot (\(\text{PathLength}_{\text{ML}}\) vs \(\text{PathLength}_{\text{AP}}\)) with confidence ellipses. * Panel C: Total path length density distributions by condition faceted across age groups.

R (patchwork)Python (matplotlib & seaborn)




Show Code
# Panel A: Age Histogram
FigA <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "grey", col = "black", binwidth = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(15, 90), breaks = seq(10, 90, 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))

# Panel B: ML vs AP Path Length Scatter
FigB <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = PathLength_ML, y = PathLength_AP)) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = Condition), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.4, col = "black") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = Condition), col = "black", shape = 21, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Path Length M/L (cm)", y = "Path Length A/P (cm)") +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"), legend.position = "none")

# Panel C: Density Distributions by Condition
FigC <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, aes(x = PathLength_Total)) +
  geom_density(aes(fill = Condition), alpha = 0.4, col = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Total Path Length (cm)", y = "Density") +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

# Combine Panels via Patchwork
((FigA + FigB) / FigC) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A') & 
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 14))

title: Data Import & Quality Assurance
text:
1 Import and Merge Data
As mentioned before, we will be using the data from this study by Santos & Duarte (2016). If you want to run the code below on your local machine, please follow the links in their PeerJ article to download their data from FigShare. Alternatively, if you just want to follow along with the code, you can see all of the code, outputs, and figures below without having to download any data.
If you do download the data, please save it in this structure:
YOUR_FOLDER_HERE/               # Name of the project folder on your local computer
└── data/                       # data subfolder
    └── BDS/                
        ├── trials/              # These are the individual trials data files downloaded from Figshare
            └── BDS00001.csv         # 60s of stabilometer data for trial 1
            └── ...
            └── BDS01956.csv         # 60s of stabilometer data for trial 1956
        └── output/             # This is where we will store outputs generated by the code
        └── BDSinfo.csv         # This is the demographic datafile from FigShare. This file maps trials to subjects.
        # Note that on figshare, the BDSinfo.csv is in the same folder as the individual trial data
        # we move it out of that folder to make some of our automated steps easier.
        
        
Note that our data differ from the original Santos & Duarte (2016) dataset. The original data were collected and processed to a very high standard to maximize their utility for biomechanics researchers. Because we want to use these data for teaching purposes, we manipulated some of the original data to introduce artifacts and other types of errors that we want to catch in our pipeline. Thus, the data presented below are for teaching purposes only and we explicitly do not make the “doctored” data available to avoid confusion with the original dataset. If readers are interested in following along step by step, they should download the original data from their source, but remember that those data will not include the errors we built in for teaching purposes.
In the code chunks below, you can toggle between the R and Python implementations. We have tried to keep the code as similar as possible between the two languages, but it is important to remember that:

There is never only one way to things in programming, although some ways are better than others (and we try to show only “good” ways).
Each programming language is different. So, even though we try to keep the code as structurally similar as possible, there often won’t be a one-to-one translation between languages.

In the chunks below, we show the structure of the “raw” data after they have been merged into one master data files (rather than individual .csv files for every subject on every trial).

R (tidyverse & data.table)Python (pandas & pyarrow)




Show Code
library(reticulate)
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(arrow)

# 1. Read metadata
info_path <- "./data/BDS/BDSinfo.txt"
info_raw  <- read_tsv(info_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

info <- info_raw %>%
  select(Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, Age, AgeGroup, Gender, Height, Weight, BMI) %>%
  mutate(
    Subject  = as.integer(Subject),
    Vision   = factor(Vision, levels = c("Open", "Closed")),
    Surface  = factor(Surface, levels = c("Firm", "Foam")),
    AgeGroup = factor(AgeGroup),
    Gender   = factor(Gender)
  )

# 2. Batch-read raw trial files
trial_files <- list.files("./data/BDS/trials", pattern = "^BDS\\d+\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)
trial_ids   <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(trial_files))

read_one_trial <- function(path, trial_id) {
  fread(path, header = TRUE, sep = "\t", showProgress = FALSE) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    rename_with(~ str_trim(str_remove(.x, "\\[.*\\]"))) %>%
    mutate(Trial = trial_id, .before = 1)
}

trial_list <- map2(trial_files, trial_ids, read_one_trial)
all_trials <- bind_rows(trial_list)

# 3. Merge & Save
master <- all_trials %>%
  left_join(info, by = "Trial") %>%
  relocate(Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, Age, AgeGroup, Gender, Height, Weight, BMI, .before = Time)

dir.create("./data/BDS/output", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
arrow::write_parquet(master, "./data/BDS/output/BDS_master.parquet")
glimpse(master)

2 Quality Assurance & Feature Extraction
From raw Center of Pressure (COP) time-series data \((COP_x, COP_y)\), we will calculate key biomechanical variables that a researcher might be interested in:

Path Lengths: Sum of absolute step distances across axes: \[\text{PathLength}_{\text{AP}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} |COP_{y, n+1} - COP_{y, n}|\] \[\text{PathLength}_{\text{Total}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} \sqrt{(COP_{x, n+1} - COP_{x, n})^2 + (COP_{y, n+1} - COP_{y, n})^2}\]
95% Confidence Ellipse Area & Boundary: \[\text{Area}_{95} = 2 \pi F_{0.95, 2, N-2} \sqrt{\lambda_1 \lambda_2}\] where \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) are eigenvalues of the \((COP_x, COP_y)\) covariance matrix.
Mean Velocity: The average of the change in center of pressure in anterior-posterior (AP) and medial-lateral (ML) axes separately.

Before visualizing these features, we also flag a few common structural and signal-level problems that occur in this kind of research. Each flag targets a different stage where something can go wrong:

flag_sample_count – does this trial have roughly the expected number of samples? Trials were meant to run 60s at 100Hz (6,000 samples), so we compare each trial’s row count to the modal count across all trials and flag anything off by more than 10 samples. This is a completeness check: did the recording actually capture the full trial, or did it start late, end early, or get truncated when the file was written to disk?
flag_time_gap – within a trial, does Time advance smoothly at the expected ~0.01s interval, with no backward jumps or repeats? This is a temporal integrity check: it catches dropped samples or corrupted timestamps. This matters more than it might seem, because path-length and velocity are both computed from consecutive-sample differences – a silent gap in time doesn’t just look wrong, it quietly inflates those estimates without ever producing an obviously “broken” value.
flag_fz_unweighting – does the vertical force (Fz) ever drop well below what’s typical for that trial? Fz roughly tracks how much of the participant’s body weight is loading the plate, so a sustained drop below 70% of the trial’s median suggests the participant wasn’t fully weight-bearing for part of the trial – a partial step off, a hand momentarily on a rail, or (especially relevant in older or clinical populations) a spotter briefly providing support. Unlike the first two flags, this one isn’t about the recording – it’s about whether the trial was performed the way the protocol intended.

We combine these into a single flag_any column so we have one place to filter for problem trials.
Errors like these are common in this kind of research simply because of scale: a large postural-sway study generates many independently-recorded, largely unattended trials – here, 163 participants x 12 trials each – and at that volume, rare per-trial failure rates become guaranteed somewhere in the dataset. Hardware and software issues (a force plate briefly losing connection, a buffer overflow, a file that didn’t finish writing) and participant/protocol issues (stepping off the plate, needing brief physical support) are each individually uncommon but collectively inevitable across thousands of trials – which is exactly why we build automated checks into the pipeline rather than relying on a raw export being clean.
In the plots below, we show how we can visualize “trial-level” data, calculated across all 60s in each trial, in each condition. This is a high-level summary plot that allows you to visualize data from many different participants at once. This kind of plot would be useful identifying influential participants who do not fit general patterns and may even be considered “outliers”. For instance, only one participant has a total path length over 600 in the eyes closed/foam surface condition. It would be worth checking notes from the data collection to see if there was an anomaly in the testing that might explain why this person is a statistical outlier. Broadly, we do not recommend removing outliers for statistical reasons alone (e.g., there will always be an extreme 1%, so we cannot remove it for its extreme-ness alone), but identifying statistical outliers is often a useful first step in ensuring data quality.

compute_path_metrics <- function(x, y, duration_s) {
  dx <- diff(x)
  dy <- diff(y)
  pl_ml    <- sum(abs(dx))
  pl_ap    <- sum(abs(dy))
  pl_total <- sum(sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2))
  
  tibble(
    PathLength_AP    = pl_ap,
    PathLength_ML    = pl_ml,
    PathLength_Total = pl_total,
    MeanVelocity_AP  = pl_ap / duration_s,
    MeanVelocity_ML  = pl_ml / duration_s
  )
}

compute_ellipse95 <- function(x, y) {
  n <- length(x)
  cov_mat <- stats::cov(cbind(x, y))
  eig <- eigen(cov_mat)
  Fval <- stats::qf(0.95, df1 = 2, df2 = n - 2)
  area <- 2 * pi * Fval * sqrt(eig$values[1] * eig$values[2])
  
  list(area = area, eig = eig, Fval = Fval, center = c(mean(x), mean(y)))
}

ellipse_boundary_df <- function(x, y, n_points = 100) {
  e <- compute_ellipse95(x, y)
  axis_lengths <- sqrt(2 * e$Fval * e$eig$values)
  theta  <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n_points)
  circle <- rbind(cos(theta), sin(theta))
  pts <- e$eig$vectors %*% diag(axis_lengths) %*% circle
  
  tibble(ex = e$center[1] + pts[1, ], ey = e$center[2] + pts[2, ])
}

compute_trial_features <- function(df) {
  n        <- nrow(df)
  duration <- max(df$Time) - min(df$Time)
  path_m   <- compute_path_metrics(df$COPx, df$COPy, duration)
  ellipse  <- compute_ellipse95(df$COPx, df$COPy)
  time_d   <- diff(df$Time)
  
  bind_cols(
    path_m,
    tibble(
      EllipseArea95     = ellipse$area,
      n_samples         = n,
      duration_s        = duration,
      Fz_min            = min(df$Fz),
      Fz_median         = median(df$Fz),
      time_gap_max      = max(time_d),
      time_nonmonotonic = any(time_d <= 0)
    )
  )
}

title: Interactive Data Visualization
text:
1 Introduction
While static graphics are ideal for publication, interactive visualizations are essential for data exploration and quality assurance (QA). Interactive tooltips allow researchers to inspect individual outliers, verify data flags, and examine subject metadata without cluttering the plot canvas.
In this module, we demonstrate how to build interactive figures: * In R, we use ggiraph, which extends ggplot2 syntax by converting standard geoms into interactive HTML elements. * In Python, we use plotly (plotly.express and plotly.graph_objects), which creates web-ready JavaScript widgets from pandas DataFrames.



2 Interactive Postural Sway Across Conditions
In this first example, we make our multi-condition postural sway trajectories interactive. Hovering over any point displays subject metadata (Subject ID, Age, Gender, and Total Path Length), and hovering over an individual point highlights the subject’s entire trajectory across conditions.

R (ggplot2 & ggiraph)Python (plotly)




Show Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggiraph)

# 1. Load Summary Data & Aggregate to Subject Averages
DATA <- readRDS("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.rds") %>% 
  mutate(
    Subject  = factor(Subject),
    AgeGroup = fct_relevel(AgeGroup, "Young", "Old")
  )

AVE_DATA <- DATA %>% 
  select(-Trial) %>%
  group_by(Subject, Vision, Surface) %>%
  summarise(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    across(!where(is.numeric), dplyr::first),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Condition = factor(paste0(Surface, ":", Vision),
                       levels = c("Firm:Open", "Firm:Closed", "Foam:Open", "Foam:Closed"))
  )

# 2. Build Tooltip Text
AVE_DATA <- AVE_DATA %>%
  mutate(tooltip_text = paste0(
    "<b>Subject ID:</b> ", Subject, "<br>",
    "<b>Age:</b> ", round(Age, 1), " years<br>",
    "<b>Gender:</b> ", Gender, "<br>",
    "<b>Sway (Path Length):</b> ", round(PathLength_Total, 1), " cm"
  ))

# 3. Define Colorblind Palette
cbPalette <- c("#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99")

# 4. Create Interactive ggplot
p_sway <- ggplot(data = AVE_DATA, 
                 aes(x = Condition, y = PathLength_Total,
                     tooltip = tooltip_text, data_id = Subject)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Subject),
            color = "gray75", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5,
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.2)) +
  geom_point_interactive(aes(shape = Condition, col = Condition, group = Subject), 
                         size = 2.5, alpha = 0.7, position = position_dodge(width = 0.2),
                         hover_nearest = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ AgeGroup) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = cbPalette) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = cbPalette) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects",
    subtitle = "Hover points to inspect subject metadata; lines connect individual trajectories",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total Path Length (cm)",
    shape = "Condition", col = "Condition", fill = "Condition"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, face = "italic", color = "gray30"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

# 5. Render Interactive girafe Widget
girafe(
  ggobj = p_sway,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:red;stroke:black;r:5pt;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;"),
    opts_tooltip(css = "background-color:black;color:white;padding:8px;border-radius:4px;font-family:sans-serif;")
  )
)

import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# 1. Load Summary Data & Aggregate to Subject Averages
DATA = pd.read_csv("./data/BDS/output/BDS_trial_summary.csv")
DATA["AgeGroup"] = pd.Categorical(DATA["AgeGroup"], categories=["Young", "Old"], ordered=True)

meta_cols = ["Subject", "Vision", "Surface", "AgeGroup", "Gender"]
AVE_DATA = DATA.groupby(meta_cols, as_index=False, observed=True).mean(numeric_only=True)
AVE_DATA["Condition"] = AVE_DATA["Surface"].astype(str) + ":" + AVE_DATA["Vision"].astype(str)

cond_order = ["Firm:Open", "Firm:Closed", "Foam:Open", "Foam:Closed"]
cbPalette = ["#1E6654", "#CC5500", "#954535", "#5B7C99"]
cond_colors = {cond: cbPalette[i] for i, cond in enumerate(cond_order)}

# 2. Build Base Scatter Plot
fig1 = px.scatter(
    AVE_DATA,
    x="Condition",
    y="PathLength_Total",
    color="Condition",
    symbol="Condition",
    facet_col="AgeGroup",
    category_orders={"AgeGroup": ["Young", "Old"], "Condition": cond_order},
    color_discrete_map=cond_colors,
    custom_data=["Subject", "Age", "Gender", "PathLength_Total"],
    labels={"PathLength_Total": "Total Path Length (cm)", "Condition": "Condition"},
    title="<b>Postural Sway: Between- and Within-Subject Effects</b><br><sup>Hover points to inspect subject metadata; lines connect individual trajectories</sup>"
)

# 3. Add Within-Subject Trajectory Lines Across Subplots
for i, age_grp in enumerate(["Young", "Old"], start=1):
    sub_df = AVE_DATA[AVE_DATA["AgeGroup"] == age_grp]
    for sub_id, grp in sub_df.groupby("Subject"):

)

3 Interactive Quality Assurance (Force Plate Calibration & Unweighting)
In this second example, we evaluate force plate calibration and screen for potential artifacts (such as a participant stepping off or unweighting the platform).
Under static gravity, vertical force \(F_z\) should approximate body weight in Newtons:
\[F_z \approx \text{Mass (kg)} \times 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2\]
Hovering over flagged data points instantly reveals trial parameters, recorded body weight, and minimum vs. median \(F_z\) values.

title: Best Practices for Scientific Figures
text:
Up to this point, our guide has focused on producing individual figures in R and Python, whether they are static plots, interactive plots, and animated plots. This final chapter steps back from any particular tool or language to cover something more fundamental - the properties that make a figure succeed or fail once it leaves your screen and becomes printed page, a slide at a conference, or an animated .gif (aside: Do you pronounce that “Giff” or “Jiff”?). These principles discussed on this page apply broadly, whether the figure came from ggplot2, matplotlib, or a microscope.
Rather than invent this framework from scratch, we build this chapter around a widely-cited, freely available reference: Rougier, Droettboom, and Bourne’s “Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures” (PLOS Computational Biology, 2014). The article is released under a CC0 public-domain dedication, so we encourage you to read it in full. We summarize its ten rules below, then go into more technical depth on four of them that come up often in practice: adapting a figure’s resolution to its medium, choosing between raster and vector formats, assembling multi-panel figures that combine photographs and data plots, and using color responsibly.



Know your audience. Often you will want different attributes for a figure you use in a lab meeting versus a journal article versus a talk to the general-public.
Identify your message. Decide what the figure needs to say before you decide how it should look. A good figure makes both the question being asked, and the answer to that question, very clear.
Adapt the figure to its medium. A poster, a projected slide, and a printed page have different resolution, size, and legibility requirements.
Captions are not optional. The caption carries explanation the figure itself cannot - e.g., exact values, what a color or symbol means, or why a highlighted region matters.
Do not trust the defaults. Every plotting library’s default settings are good enough for many plot, but they probably are not the best settings for any specific plot.
Use color effectively. There is tremendous creative appeal in making our figures as colorful as possible, but every color choice should have a reason; if it doesn’t, use black or gray instead. Color should also generally backed up by other aesthetics (e.g., very lines but color and dash, points by color and shape) to ensure readability.
Do not mislead the reader. Many features of plot exist, despite a wide body of evidence showing they actually make plots harder to understand or even misleading (e.g., truncated axes, pie charts, and 3-D charts are generally bad practices that should be avoided).
Avoid “chartjunk.” Unnecessary gridlines, decorative colors, and redundant labels crowd out the actual signal.
Message trumps beauty. A figure’s top priorities are to be correct and legible, any attractive/aesthetic consideration should come second.
Get the right tool. Although it is efficient to have everything in a single pipieline, the software you used to analyze your data does not have to be the software you use to illustrate it.

The next four sections expand on Rules 3, 6, and 10, since resolution, color, and tool choice are where we see the common but avoidable mistakes.



DPI (dots per inch) is not a property of a file on its own - it is only meaningful once you also know the physical size at which the file will be printed or displayed. A 3,000-pixel-wide image is 1,000 DPI at a 3-inch width and only 300 DPI at a 10-inch width. This is why a figure that looks perfectly sharp on a laptop screen (which usually renders around 72 pixels per inch) can turn blurry once it is actually printed. As a result, journals typically require 300-1200 DPI depending on content type. As a rule of thumb: photographs and other continuous-tone images are generally acceptable at 300 DPI, but line art - graphs, diagrams, anything with fine lines or small text - will be better at 600 DPI or larger, because sharp edges “alias” (i.e., turn jagged) at lower resolutions in a way smooth photographic tones do not.
The most common way people get this wrong is exporting a figure at its on-screen size (which defaults to something like 72-96 DPI) and never revisiting it, or trying to fix a low-resolution image by increasing its reported DPI after the fact. Neither adds real detail - the only reliable fix is to re-export from the original plotting code at the correct physical size and DPI together.
This is also why it helps to think you audience in advance of making a figure. For instance, you might often have “quick and dirty” figures that you churn out during a project (e.g., our quality assurance figures for individual subjects from Section 01) and these will be just fine at 72 DPI. But once you start to build figures you want in your publication, you will want to increase the resoultion at which you are exporting your figures.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# ggsave() lets you set physical size AND resolution together -- always set
# both, since DPI alone is meaningless without a physical size to pair it with.
ggsave("figure1.png", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# Line art (plots with fine ticks/text) typically needs a higher DPI than
# photographs. When in doubt, 600 DPI is a safer default for a data figure.
ggsave("figure1_lineart.tiff", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 600)






Show Code
# figsize (inches) sets the physical size; dpi determines how many pixels
# that becomes. Always set both together, same logic as ggsave() above.
fig.savefig("figure1.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

# Line art wants a higher DPI than photographs.
fig.savefig("figure1_lineart.tiff", dpi=600, bbox_inches="tight")








Compute graphics fall broadly into one of two types: raster images or vector images. Raster images are built from a fixed grid of pixels. If you enlarge the image past its original resolution, it visibly start to pixelate, because there is no more information to draw on and it has to extrapolate/interpolate the new pixels. In constract, vector images are built from mathematical descriptions of lines, curves, and shapes instead of pixels, so they can be scaled to any size - as big as a poster or as small a thumbnail - without any loss of sharpness.
For data figures specifically, this maps cleanly onto content type. Anything that is fundamentally geometric - line plots, bar charts, scatter plots, diagrams, schematics - is often best exported as a vector format (PDF, SVG, or EPS) whenever the destination allows it, because vector images sidestep the entire DPI conversation (i.e., a vector figure is sharp at whatever size). Raster images, however, remain necessary for photographs, micrographs, and anything else with continuous tonal gradation, because there is no vector geometry (or at least no simple vectorization!) to describe these complexities. Many journals now explicitly prefer PDF/EPS for line-art submissions and TIFF for photographic content, for exactly this reason. However, be sure to check your journals instructions for authors to get their specific requirements for image formats and resolutions.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# Vector formats are resolution-independent -- no DPI setting needed.
ggsave("figure1.pdf", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
ggsave("figure1.svg", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")






Show Code
# matplotlib infers the output format from the file extension.
fig.savefig("figure1.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("figure1.svg", bbox_inches="tight")





One caveat: a “vector” figure that contains an embedded raster element (a photo overlaid with vector annotations, for instance) still needs that raster component checked at the correct DPI for its final print size - wrapping something in a vector container does not retroactively fix its resolution.



A common situation in rehabilitation and movement science is combining a data figure (a stabilogram, a time series) with a photograph - maybe the experimental setup, a piece of equipment, or a histology slide. Adobe Illustrator handles this well as does the open-source program Inkscape. Regardless of the software or specific image types, there are some common principles to guide the workflow:

Export each panel individually, at its intended final size, in the appropriate format - vector (PDF/SVG) for plots, high-resolution raster (TIFF) for photos.
Do photo editing first, separately. Crop, adjust brightness/contrast, and retouch photographs in a raster editor (GIMP or Photoshop) before bringing them into the panel layout - many journals prohibit digital manipulation of photographic data after the fact, so it is best handled once, up front, and documented.
Import everything into one vector document. Bring both the vector plots and the prepared raster photos into Inkscape or Illustrator as separate objects.
Align panels deliberately, try using the editor’s alignment tools rather than dragging by eye alone. (Often it is only too late that I realize my panels are slightly “off” with one panel several pixels above or below its neighbor in the final print figure.).
Keep typography consistent across panels. A figure combining a ggplot2 panel, a matplotlib panel, and a photo’s caption text in three different fonts and sizes reads as unpolished even if every individual panel is well made; pick one font family and one or two font sizes for the whole composite.
Add a label to each panel so the caption and in-text references can point to specific panels unambiguously. Journals may differ in their required format (e.g. requiring uppercase letter, lowercase letters, or Roman numerals).
Export the assembled composite once, at the destination’s final specifications, rather than re-exporting individual panels repeatedly and re-assembling.

If you find yourself doing this often, the Scientific Inkscape extension set is worth exploring - it adds tools specifically aimed at this workflow, including a Scaler that resizes an imported plot without distorting its text and tick marks, and a Homogenizer that enforces uniform fonts and stroke widths across panels pulled in from different source figures (i.e., the “three fonts in one figure” problem explained in step 5 above).



Color is one of the easiest places to unintentionally distort or obscure your own data, so it is worth addressing deliberately rather than accepting whatever a plotting library defaults to. Colormaps fall into three functional categories, and picking the wrong category for your data type is a common, avoidable mistake:

Sequential – one color varying from light to dark (or vice versa), for quantitative data that runs low to high (e.g., path length, age).
Diverging – two colors meeting at a neutral midpoint, for data with a meaningful center to deviate from (e.g., a difference score, correlation coefficients going in opposite directions).
Qualitative – visually distinct, unordered colors, for categorical/grouping variables (e.g., Vision, Surface in our examples).

The simple rainbow (or “jet”) colormap - still a default in many plotting libraries - fails on both counts at once: it is qualitative-looking but frequently applied to sequential data, and it is not perceptually uniform, meaning equal steps in the underlying data do not produce equal steps in perceived color. Crameri, Shephard, and Heron’s “The misuse of colour in science communication” (Nature Communications, 2020) quantifies this distortion directly: an uneven color gradient can visually misrepresent the total data range and it can obscure real structure in the data behind arbitrary color banding. Their recommended alternative is a perceptually uniform sequential palette - viridis (and its relatives, magma, plasma, cividis) is the most widely adopted example, originally built for matplotlib and now available as a default or package option in nearly every plotting environment.
Color vision deficiency is the second major consideration, and it affects a meaningful fraction of any audience - roughly 8% of men have red-green color blindness, which makes red/green the single most common accidental pairing to avoid. For categorical data, the Okabe-Ito palette (popularized by Bang Wong’s 2011 Nature Methods piece, “Points of view: Color blindness”) remains distinguishable across all three common types of color vision deficiency and has become close to a de facto standard for qualitative scientific figures.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# Sequential/continuous data: viridis is perceptually uniform and
# colorblind-safe, and ships as a built-in ggplot2 scale.
ggplot(DATA, aes(x = COPx, y = COPy, color = Time)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_c()

# Categorical data: the Okabe-Ito palette, specified directly by hex code.
okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
               "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")

ggplot(DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total, color = Vision)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito)






Show Code
# Sequential/continuous data: viridis is built into matplotlib directly.
ax.scatter(DATA["COPx"], DATA["COPy"], c=DATA["Time"], cmap="viridis")

# Categorical data: the Okabe-Ito palette, specified directly by hex code.
okabe_ito = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
             "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000"]

sns.scatterplot(data=DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total",
                 hue="Vision", palette=okabe_ito)





As with the rest of Rule 6: if a color choice isn’t doing real work - distinguishing groups, encoding a value, drawing the eye to something specific - it is usually better left out, in favor of black or gray. Additionally, it is generally good practice to “back up” your color choices with another aesthetic feature. For instance, if you have lines that differ by color, consider adding dashes to them as well. Similarly, if you have points that differ by color, it is often good to give them different shapes as well. This not only helps with accessibility - overcoming color vision deficiency - but generally makes your plots more interpretable. For instance, when making a plot for a talk, always consider someone stuck in the back row of your audience, can they cleanly see everything that is going on in your plot?

Use color effectively. There is tremendous creative appeal in making our figures as colorful as possible, but every color choice should have a reason; if it doesn’t, use black or gray instead. Color should also generally backed up by other aesthetics (e.g., very lines but color and dash, points by color and shape) to ensure readability.
Do not mislead the reader. Many features of plot exist, despite a wide body of evidence showing they actually make plots harder to understand or even misleading (e.g., truncated axes, pie charts, and 3-D charts are generally bad practices that should be avoided).
Avoid “chartjunk.” Unnecessary gridlines, decorative colors, and redundant labels crowd out the actual signal.
Message trumps beauty. A figure’s top priorities are to be correct and legible, any attractive/aesthetic consideration should come second.
Get the right tool. Although it is efficient to have everything in a single pipieline, the software you used to analyze your data does not have to be the software you use to illustrate it.

The next four sections expand on Rules 3, 6, and 10, since resolution, color, and tool choice are where we see the common but avoidable mistakes.

title: Best Practices for Scientific Figures
text:
DPI (dots per inch) is not a property of a file on its own - it is only meaningful once you also know the physical size at which the file will be printed or displayed. A 3,000-pixel-wide image is 1,000 DPI at a 3-inch width and only 300 DPI at a 10-inch width. This is why a figure that looks perfectly sharp on a laptop screen (which usually renders around 72 pixels per inch) can turn blurry once it is actually printed. As a result, journals typically require 300-1200 DPI depending on content type. As a rule of thumb: photographs and other continuous-tone images are generally acceptable at 300 DPI, but line art - graphs, diagrams, anything with fine lines or small text - will be better at 600 DPI or larger, because sharp edges “alias” (i.e., turn jagged) at lower resolutions in a way smooth photographic tones do not.
The most common way people get this wrong is exporting a figure at its on-screen size (which defaults to something like 72-96 DPI) and never revisiting it, or trying to fix a low-resolution image by increasing its reported DPI after the fact. Neither adds real detail - the only reliable fix is to re-export from the original plotting code at the correct physical size and DPI together.
This is also why it helps to think you audience in advance of making a figure. For instance, you might often have “quick and dirty” figures that you churn out during a project (e.g., our quality assurance figures for individual subjects from Section 01) and these will be just fine at 72 DPI. But once you start to build figures you want in your publication, you will want to increase the resoultion at which you are exporting your figures.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# ggsave() lets you set physical size AND resolution together -- always set
# both, since DPI alone is meaningless without a physical size to pair it with.
ggsave("figure1.png", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# Line art (plots with fine ticks/text) typically needs a higher DPI than
# photographs. When in doubt, 600 DPI is a safer default for a data figure.
ggsave("figure1_lineart.tiff", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 600)






Show Code
# figsize (inches) sets the physical size; dpi determines how many pixels
# that becomes. Always set both together, same logic as ggsave() above.
fig.savefig("figure1.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

# Line art wants a higher DPI than photographs.
fig.savefig("figure1_lineart.tiff", dpi=600, bbox_inches="tight")

title: Best Practices for Scientific Figures
text:
Compute graphics fall broadly into one of two types: raster images or vector images. Raster images are built from a fixed grid of pixels. If you enlarge the image past its original resolution, it visibly start to pixelate, because there is no more information to draw on and it has to extrapolate/interpolate the new pixels. In constract, vector images are built from mathematical descriptions of lines, curves, and shapes instead of pixels, so they can be scaled to any size - as big as a poster or as small a thumbnail - without any loss of sharpness.
For data figures specifically, this maps cleanly onto content type. Anything that is fundamentally geometric - line plots, bar charts, scatter plots, diagrams, schematics - is often best exported as a vector format (PDF, SVG, or EPS) whenever the destination allows it, because vector images sidestep the entire DPI conversation (i.e., a vector figure is sharp at whatever size). Raster images, however, remain necessary for photographs, micrographs, and anything else with continuous tonal gradation, because there is no vector geometry (or at least no simple vectorization!) to describe these complexities. Many journals now explicitly prefer PDF/EPS for line-art submissions and TIFF for photographic content, for exactly this reason. However, be sure to check your journals instructions for authors to get their specific requirements for image formats and resolutions.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# Vector formats are resolution-independent -- no DPI setting needed.
ggsave("figure1.pdf", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
ggsave("figure1.svg", plot = p, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")






Show Code
# matplotlib infers the output format from the file extension.
fig.savefig("figure1.pdf", bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("figure1.svg", bbox_inches="tight")





One caveat: a “vector” figure that contains an embedded raster element (a photo overlaid with vector annotations, for instance) still needs that raster component checked at the correct DPI for its final print size - wrapping something in a vector container does not retroactively fix its resolution.

title: Best Practices for Scientific Figures
text:
A common situation in rehabilitation and movement science is combining a data figure (a stabilogram, a time series) with a photograph - maybe the experimental setup, a piece of equipment, or a histology slide. Adobe Illustrator handles this well as does the open-source program Inkscape. Regardless of the software or specific image types, there are some common principles to guide the workflow:

Export each panel individually, at its intended final size, in the appropriate format - vector (PDF/SVG) for plots, high-resolution raster (TIFF) for photos.
Do photo editing first, separately. Crop, adjust brightness/contrast, and retouch photographs in a raster editor (GIMP or Photoshop) before bringing them into the panel layout - many journals prohibit digital manipulation of photographic data after the fact, so it is best handled once, up front, and documented.
Import everything into one vector document. Bring both the vector plots and the prepared raster photos into Inkscape or Illustrator as separate objects.
Align panels deliberately, try using the editor’s alignment tools rather than dragging by eye alone. (Often it is only too late that I realize my panels are slightly “off” with one panel several pixels above or below its neighbor in the final print figure.).
Keep typography consistent across panels. A figure combining a ggplot2 panel, a matplotlib panel, and a photo’s caption text in three different fonts and sizes reads as unpolished even if every individual panel is well made; pick one font family and one or two font sizes for the whole composite.
Add a label to each panel so the caption and in-text references can point to specific panels unambiguously. Journals may differ in their required format (e.g. requiring uppercase letter, lowercase letters, or Roman numerals).
Export the assembled composite once, at the destination’s final specifications, rather than re-exporting individual panels repeatedly and re-assembling.

If you find yourself doing this often, the Scientific Inkscape extension set is worth exploring - it adds tools specifically aimed at this workflow, including a Scaler that resizes an imported plot without distorting its text and tick marks, and a Homogenizer that enforces uniform fonts and stroke widths across panels pulled in from different source figures (i.e., the “three fonts in one figure” problem explained in step 5 above).

title: Best Practices for Scientific Figures
text:
Color is one of the easiest places to unintentionally distort or obscure your own data, so it is worth addressing deliberately rather than accepting whatever a plotting library defaults to. Colormaps fall into three functional categories, and picking the wrong category for your data type is a common, avoidable mistake:

Sequential – one color varying from light to dark (or vice versa), for quantitative data that runs low to high (e.g., path length, age).
Diverging – two colors meeting at a neutral midpoint, for data with a meaningful center to deviate from (e.g., a difference score, correlation coefficients going in opposite directions).
Qualitative – visually distinct, unordered colors, for categorical/grouping variables (e.g., Vision, Surface in our examples).

The simple rainbow (or “jet”) colormap - still a default in many plotting libraries - fails on both counts at once: it is qualitative-looking but frequently applied to sequential data, and it is not perceptually uniform, meaning equal steps in the underlying data do not produce equal steps in perceived color. Crameri, Shephard, and Heron’s “The misuse of colour in science communication” (Nature Communications, 2020) quantifies this distortion directly: an uneven color gradient can visually misrepresent the total data range and it can obscure real structure in the data behind arbitrary color banding. Their recommended alternative is a perceptually uniform sequential palette - viridis (and its relatives, magma, plasma, cividis) is the most widely adopted example, originally built for matplotlib and now available as a default or package option in nearly every plotting environment.
Color vision deficiency is the second major consideration, and it affects a meaningful fraction of any audience - roughly 8% of men have red-green color blindness, which makes red/green the single most common accidental pairing to avoid. For categorical data, the Okabe-Ito palette (popularized by Bang Wong’s 2011 Nature Methods piece, “Points of view: Color blindness”) remains distinguishable across all three common types of color vision deficiency and has become close to a de facto standard for qualitative scientific figures.

R (ggplot2)Python (matplotlib)




Show Code
# Sequential/continuous data: viridis is perceptually uniform and
# colorblind-safe, and ships as a built-in ggplot2 scale.
ggplot(DATA, aes(x = COPx, y = COPy, color = Time)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_c()

# Categorical data: the Okabe-Ito palette, specified directly by hex code.
okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
               "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")

ggplot(DATA, aes(x = Surface, y = PathLength_Total, color = Vision)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito)






Show Code
# Sequential/continuous data: viridis is built into matplotlib directly.
ax.scatter(DATA["COPx"], DATA["COPy"], c=DATA["Time"], cmap="viridis")

# Categorical data: the Okabe-Ito palette, specified directly by hex code.
okabe_ito = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
             "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000"]

sns.scatterplot(data=DATA, x="Surface", y="PathLength_Total",
                 hue="Vision", palette=okabe_ito)





As with the rest of Rule 6: if a color choice isn’t doing real work - distinguishing groups, encoding a value, drawing the eye to something specific - it is usually better left out, in favor of black or gray. Additionally, it is generally good practice to “back up” your color choices with another aesthetic feature. For instance, if you have lines that differ by color, consider adding dashes to them as well. Similarly, if you have points that differ by color, it is often good to give them different shapes as well. This not only helps with accessibility - overcoming color vision deficiency - but generally makes your plots more interpretable. For instance, when making a plot for a talk, always consider someone stuck in the back row of your audience, can they cleanly see everything that is going on in your plot?
